title: Learn by Doing: Architecture versus Organization
lead: The topic sat as a paper: the objective questions on it, then every past question the examiner has set on it, each with its model answer and the method taught from nothing.
intro:
Part A is the objective questions on this topic, the two tests' own questions first. Part B is past questions only: nothing invented, each one labelled with the year it was set and every other year it has been set in.

This topic opens almost every paper, and it is two marks you either have or do not.

lockin.big: "Architecture is what the programmer sees. Organization is how it is built."
lockin.sub: Instruction set, data types, addressing modes and registers are architecture. Control signals, buses, memory technology and how the adder is wired are organization.

methodFrames.teach: Two machines can run exactly the same programs and be built completely differently inside. That one sentence is the whole topic.
methodFrames.ask: If the programs are identical, what must be identical about the two machines?

methodFrames.check: What the programmer can see: the instructions, the registers, the way memory is addressed.
methodFrames.teach: That visible part is the architecture: the instruction set, the data types, the addressing modes and the register organization. It answers WHAT the computer does.
methodFrames.ask: So what is left over, and what question does it answer?

methodFrames.check: How it is built: the control signals, the buses, the memory technology.
methodFrames.teach: That is the organization, and it answers HOW. Two processors with the same architecture may differ entirely in organization: one may have a hardware multiplier, the other may do it by repeated addition, and the same instruction works on both.
methodFrames.ask: Which one changes more often, and why does that matter commercially?

methodFrames.check: Organization, because it can change without breaking the software.
methodFrames.teach: That is the answer worth the extra mark: the architecture is kept stable across a family of processors so that old programs still run, while the organization is improved generation by generation.
methodFrames.ask: Sort these four into the two boxes: number of general purpose registers, width of the internal data path, the set of addressing modes, the cache size.

methodFrames.check: Architecture: registers and addressing modes. Organization: data path width and cache size.
methodFrames.teach: Cache size is the one people get wrong. A cache is invisible to the instruction set: a program runs identically with a bigger one, only faster. Invisible to the programmer means organization.
methodFrames.ask: The question is worth 2 marks and says "differentiate". How should the answer be laid out?

methodFrames.check: Two labelled sentences, one for each, with an example in each.
methodFrames.teach: Never one paragraph about both. Write Architecture: then its definition and two examples, then Organization: and the same. An examiner marking to a scheme is looking for the two names and the two examples, and a table earns them fastest.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Q1(a)

scenario.text: a. i) Computer Systems are designed using two closely related but distinct concepts which are Computer Architecture and Computer Organization. Differentiate between these concepts. 2mks ii) Compare Von Neumann Architecture and Harvard Architecture. Include a diagram for each. 3mks

questions.asked: Set once, in 2025/2026. It is still the examiner's own question, and the method behind it is on the syllabus.

breakdown.question: Before you write: what are you given, what is actually asked, and what do the marks tell you about the length of the answer?
breakdown.answer: Work it out first Read the question twice, list what you are given, and say in one line what the answer will look like: a number, a table, a diagram, or a list of points. Then open the answer and mark yourself against it.

exam.problem: i) Differentiate computer architecture from computer organization.
exam.answer:
Computer architecture is defined as the functional design and logical structure of the computer system as the programmer sees it: the instruction set, the data types, the addressing modes and the register organization. It answers the question "What does the computer do?" and serves as the blueprint for the system.

Computer organization is defined as the operational units and their interconnections that realize (carry out) that architecture: the control signals, the buses, the memory technology used and the cache. It answers the question "How does the computer do it?" A useful likeness: architecture is the building's design, organization is the actual construction of the building.

ii) Compare Von Neumann and Harvard architecture, with a diagram for each.

Von Neumann architecture is defined as a design that uses a single (shared) area of memory, reached over one bus, for both the program instructions and the data those instructions act on. It is simple to build, but the shared path is a bottleneck (an instruction fetch and a data access cannot happen at the same instant).

Harvard architecture is defined as a design that uses separate memories and separate buses for instructions and data, which lets it fetch an instruction and read data at the same time (a form of parallelism), at the cost of duplicating the address, data and control lines.
